title: Offsite snapshot strategy, failover runbook and Terraform state notes for private deployments
content:
Purpose and scope:
This working doc captures an operationally-focused approach for offsite snapshots, failover procedures, and Terraform state hygiene for private (VPC / on-prem) Redwood deployments. It is deliberately pragmatic: aimed at SREs and platform engineers who must recover a customer environment from catastrophic infrastructure failure (site-loss, major storage corruption, or operator error).

Goals / targets:
- RTO target tiers: 15m (critical control plane only), 1h (core inference path), 6h (non-critical analytics).
- RPO target tiers: continuous WAL for databases (<=1m), incremental object-store snapshots hourly, full image snapshots daily.
- Safe upgrade posture: always take golden snapshots + terraform state snapshot before any control-plane or infra upgrade.

Assumptions / constraints:
- Private deployments vary: some on customer-hosted VMs, others in customer VPCs pointing to object store endpoints (S3-compatible).
- We do not assume cross-cloud control-plane access in outages; DR relies on pre-configured offsite storage and documented key escrow.
- KMS keys may be customer-managed; DR playbook includes key-recovery steps.

Architecture summary (recommended patterns):
1) Control plane (control-plane-api, operator-state): keep nightly AMI/VM snapshots + offsite object-store backup of manifests and secrets (encrypted).
2) Databases: primary PostgreSQL with continuous WAL shipping to offsite storage or replica in DR location. Prefer logical replication + base backups retained for 30 days.
3) Object store: point-in-time object snapshots (versioned buckets) plus lifecycle rules to retain critical artifacts for 90 days.
4) Cache & KV: Redis RDB snapshots every 5m (if available) + async AOF offsite copy; for critical caches, plan for rebuildable fallback strategies.
5) Terraform state: remote backend (S3/GCS/MinIO) with state locking (DynamoDB/etcd/consul). Backups of state file taken before changes and on schedule.

Offsite snapshot cadence (recommended):
- Control plane manifests/helm values: push to git + nightly tarball to offsite object-store (encrypted).
- Full VM images: daily at 02:00 UTC, retain 14 days.
- Block volume incremental snapshots: every 6h for critical tenants; daily for others.
- Database basebackup: daily; WAL shipping continuous; verify WAL apply by hourly probe on replica.

Pre-DR preparations (checklist to maintain weekly):
- Verify object-store credentials and test list/get to offsite bucket.
- Confirm terraform backend still reachable and lock/unlock test passes.
- Verify KMS/HSM key backups or key-escrow procedure and record holder contact.
- Confirm runbook phone tree and escalation list up-to-date.
- Run a table-top DR review once per quarter and a full drill every 6 months.

Terraform module notes (state hygiene & DR):
- Backend recommendations: use a bucket with versioning enabled + server-side encryption. Put a lifecycle that snapshots every state change to a separate retention prefix.
- Locking: enable a consistent lock (DynamoDB for S3, or Consul for MinIO) to avoid state corruption during failover work.
- Pre-change snapshot command: terraform state pull > backups/state-YYYYMMDD-HHMM.tfstate and upload to offsite bucket.
- Automated state snapshots: a periodic job (cron) that runs terraform state pull for each workspace and archives N last versions to offsite store.
- Migration notes: when migrating backends, follow terraform recommended state mv procedure and keep 3 copies of the state file in different offsite locations until confirmed.
- Secrets: avoid embedding secrets in state; when unavoidable, encrypt state at rest and keep separate KMS key backups.

Example backend snippet (reference, adapt to customer):
- backend "s3" {
    bucket = "redwood-private-state-<tenant>"
    key    = "envs/prod/terraform.tfstate"
    region = "us-west-2"
    kms_key_id = "arn:aws:kms:...:key/xxxxx"
  }
(Also ensure bucket versioning = true and a lifecycle rule to move older versions to cold storage after 30 days.)

Upgrade & pre-upgrade checklist (must be done before any infra or operator upgrade):
1) Create golden snapshot of control plane and databases.
2) Run terraform state snapshot (see module notes) and commit to offsite backup.
3) Run smoke tests against a staging replica; confirm inference latency within SLO.
4) Pause automated jobs (backups etc.) that might interfere with upgrade windows.
5) Document the exact PR and terraform plan and attach runbook ticket.

Failover runbook (ordered, copy to incident channel):
Trigger: site-unreachable OR confirmed storage corruption OR critical data-plane failure.
A) Incident declaration (T0):
- Eng lead declares DR mode in incident channel and pages DR on-call.
- Set an incident doc and record timeline.

B) Short-term mitigation (T0+5m):
- Update DNS TTLs to prepare for traffic cutover (lower to 30s if possible).
- If control plane reachable, mark degraded; if not, prepare DR target environment.

C) Restore object artifacts (T0+15m):
- From offsite object-store, restore the control-plane manifests tarball to DR environment.
- Commands: aws s3 cp s3://redwood-offsite/<tenant>/manifests-YYYY.tar.gz ./ && tar xzvf manifests-YYYY.tar.gz

D) Restore Terraform state (T0+20m):
- Pull latest known-good state from offsite: aws s3 cp s3://redwood-offsite/state-backups/<tenant>/latest.tfstate ./recovered.tfstate
- For safety, set a lock in the backend to prevent writes while you validate.
- If you must import resources into a new backend, follow terraform import and state replace-provider steps; prefer rehydrating VM images and re-applying minimal infra modules first.

E) Database recovery (T0+30m+):
- Restore last basebackup and apply WALs. Example sequence: restore basebackup to PG_DIR, then set recovery_target_time to last_wal_timestamp and start postgres.
- If WALs or basebackup corrupt, fallback: spin up read-replica in DR region from last available basebackup and accept RPO delta.

F) Secrets and KMS (T0+45m):
- If keys are customer-managed, coordinate with the customer to import or re-create keys in the DR KMS.
- For HSM-backed keys where import not possible, ensure re-issue of new keys and rotate application secrets accordingly.

G) Traffic cutover (T0+1h):
- Point traffic to DR endpoints by updating DNS and load balancer configs. Monitor 5xx and latencies.
- If using global load balancing, disable origin healthy checks to avoid sending traffic to failed site.

H) Post-cutover validation (T0+1h–3h):
- Run smoke suite: health endpoints, sample inference request, database read/write checks, metrics ingestion.
- Validate token-level billing counters and object-store read/write.

I) Reconciliation & restore back (post-incident):
- Once original site restored, plan a controlled failback: re-sync databases, verify data parity, and run canary traffic before final DNS flip.
- Ensure terraform state reflects new production topology before full failback.

Validation tests (quick list):
- WAL apply success on replica within 5 minutes of restore.
- A set of 20 inference queries return within 2x normal median latency.
- Storage object checksum verification for critical manifests.
- TLS certs present and valid for endpoints.

Drill cadence and metrics to collect during drills:
- Drill frequency: table-top quarterly, live full-restore every 6 months per customer.
- Measure time-to-restore (control plane, db, object-store), number of manual steps, and failed steps.
- Capture gaps (missing credentials, expired keys, missing terraform snapshots) and assign remediation.

Known gotchas and mitigation notes:
- State drift after emergency manual fixes: always record manual changes and commit a recovered state snapshot before re-applying terraform.
- KMS/HSM import constraints: if keys are non-exportable, plan for key rotation strategy rather than re-import.
- Large object-store restores can be slow; pre-warm critical artifacts by selectively restoring critical paths first (manifests, certs, minimal model weights).
- Network ACLs and firewall rules: DR targets must have pre-authorized IP ranges for operator IPs to avoid being locked out.

Post-incident checklist (what to do within 72h):
- Full postmortem with timeline and owner-assigned remediation tasks.
- Rotate any credentials or keys that were exposed or used in recovery.
- Update runbook to reflect any surprises and commit a new golden terraform state snapshot.
- Schedule a follow-up drill to validate remediations.

Appendix A — quick commands reference:
- Terraform state snapshot: terraform state pull > backups/state-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).tfstate && aws s3 cp backups/ s3://redwood-offsite/state-backups/<tenant>/ --recursive
- Database basebackup (example): pg_basebackup -h primary -D /var/lib/postgres/backup -U repl -Ft -z -P
- WAL fetch (example): wal-e --aws-instance-profile download-push wal-e
- Object restore (example): aws s3 sync s3://redwood-offsite/<tenant>/critical ./critical --delete

Appendix B — suggested terraform module checklist to include in repo (short):
- pre_change: state snapshot job hook (CI)
- post_change: automated state archive to offsite store
- dr_metadata: module exposes tags/labels indicating backup schedule and retention
- validation: module includes a small probe infra (healthcheck URL) that can be used post-restore for smoke testing

Open questions (to resolve in followup):
- Should we standardize on a single replication strategy for DBs across all private deployments or allow per-customer choices?
- What is the canonical location for our offsite KMS key escrow (internal vault vs customer-managed)?
- Do we want to implement automatic terraform state backups as part of the platform control plane?

Next steps (owners assigned):
- Priya: draft a mini-runbook checklist card for runbook binder and schedule the next drill (due in 6 weeks).
- Liam: prototype the terraform state snapshot cron job and open a PR for the modules repo.
- Ethan: coordinate with security to define KMS escrow workflow and owners.

This is a living draft — update as we run drills and find friction.
